title: Text: strings, indexing and methods
summary: Pick characters out of text, cut slices, and clean text up with string methods.
license: Original work for Python Intelligence; license to be chosen by the owner
objective: Index and slice strings, use string methods, and build new strings since strings can't be changed in place.
analogy: A string is a row of numbered tiles you can read but not repaint: to change it you lay out a new row.

misconceptions.correction: Indexes start at 0: `s[0]` is the first, `s[-1]` the last.
Strings are immutable; it returns a new string that you must keep.
The end of a slice is excluded: positions 2, 3 and 4.

rubric.evidence: indexes and slices pick exactly the characters asked for
methods like replace, strip and isdigit do the work instead of manual loops
results are new strings; inputs are left as they were

review.recall: What do `s[-1]`, `s[:3]` and `s[::-1]` give? Why doesn't `s.upper()` change s?

steps.title: Text is everywhere
steps.body:
Names, email addresses, messages, file contents and web pages are all text. Real text is messy: extra
spaces, mixed capitals, the part you want buried in the middle. This lesson gives you the tools to
reach inside a piece of text, take exactly the part you need, and tidy it up.

steps.title: A row of numbered boxes
steps.body:
Think of a string as a row of boxes with one character in each. The boxes are numbered from **0**, so
in `"code"` the `c` is in box 0 and the `e` is in box 3. You can also count from the right with
negative numbers: box `-1` is the last character.

A **slice** cuts the row between boxes. `word[1:3]` means "start cutting before box 1 and stop before
box 3", which gives the characters in boxes 1 and 2. The boxes themselves are sealed: you can read
them and make new strings from them, but you can't change a character in place.

questions: If a string has 5 characters, what is the number of its last box when counting from 0?
Why might it be useful that a slice stops *before* its end number?

steps.title: Watch a new string being built
steps.body: Strings can't be changed, so this function builds a **new** string one character at a time.

frames.note: Start with an empty string: the accumulator.
A `for` loop over a string visits each character in turn. First: 'h'.
`ch.upper()` gives a new string 'H'; joining makes a new `result`.
Second pass: 'i' becomes 'I', and `result` is now 'HI'. `word` itself never changed.

steps.title: The precise rules
steps.body:
**Indexing:** `s[i]` is the character at position `i`, counting from 0; `s[-1]` is the last one.
An index past the end raises `IndexError`. `len(s)` is the number of characters.

**Slicing:** `s[a:b]` gives the characters from position `a` up to but **not including** `b`.
Leave out `a` to start at the beginning, or `b` to go to the end: `s[:3]`, `s[3:]`. A slice never
raises `IndexError`; out-of-range ends are simply clipped. A third number is a step, so `s[::-1]`
is the string reversed.

**Immutability:** `s[0] = "x"` is a `TypeError`. No string method changes the original. Methods that
transform text (`upper`, `strip`, `replace`, ...) return a **new** string, so keep the result:
`name = name.strip()`. Others return something else: `find` a number, `split` a list, `isalpha` a bool.

**Common methods:** `upper()`, `lower()`, `strip()` (remove surrounding spaces), `replace(old, new)`,
`split()` (break into a list of words), `startswith(prefix)`, `find(sub)` (position, or `-1` if
absent), `isalpha()`. The operator `sub in s` asks whether `sub` appears anywhere in `s`.

steps.title: Run it: tidy an email address
steps.body: Predict each printed line, then **Run**. Notice that every step makes a new string.
steps.code:
email = "  Ada.Lovelace@Example.com "
clean = email.strip().lower()
print(clean)
print(clean[0])
print(clean[-3:])
user = clean[:clean.find("@")]
print(user)
print("@" in clean)

steps.title: Your turn: initials
steps.body:
Complete `initials(full_name)` so it returns the capital first letter of every word:
`initials("ada lovelace")` is `"AL"`. Extra spaces between or around words must not matter.

`full_name.split()` gives you the words as a list you can loop over.
steps.starter:
def initials(full_name):
    result = ""
    # add the first letter of each word
    return result
hints: Loop over `full_name.split()`; each item is one word.
The first letter of `word` is `word[0]`; make it a capital with `.upper()`.

tests.name: two words
tests.code: assert initials('ada lovelace') == 'AL', f"initials('ada lovelace') returned {initials('ada lovelace')!r}"

tests.name: three words
tests.code: assert initials('Grace Brewster Hopper') == 'GBH', f"got {initials('Grace Brewster Hopper')!r}"

tests.name: messy spacing
tests.code: assert initials('  alan   turing ') == 'AT', f"got {initials('  alan   turing ')!r}; split() with no argument ignores extra spaces"

steps.title: Challenge: palindromes
steps.body:
A palindrome reads the same backwards. Write `is_palindrome(text)` that returns `True` or `False`,
**ignoring capitals and anything that isn't a letter**, so `"Never odd or even"` counts.

Build a cleaned-up string first, then compare it with its reverse.
hints: The starter fails on capitals and spaces. Which characters should you keep?
Loop over `text`, keep only characters where `ch.isalpha()` is true, and lower-case them.

tests.name: simple
tests.code: assert is_palindrome('level') is True, 'level is a palindrome'

tests.name: not a palindrome
tests.code: assert is_palindrome('python') is False, 'python is not a palindrome'

tests.name: ignores case and spaces
tests.code: assert is_palindrome('Never odd or even') is True, 'ignore capitals and spaces'

tests.name: ignores punctuation
tests.code: assert is_palindrome('A man, a plan, a canal: Panama!') is True, 'ignore punctuation too'

tests.name: empty text
tests.code: assert is_palindrome('') is True, 'an empty string reads the same both ways'

steps.title: Transfer: masking a card number
steps.body:
Card numbers are often written with spaces, like `"4111 1111 1111 1234"`. Write `mask(card)`, which removes the spaces
and replaces every digit except the last four with `*`. Then write `brand(card)`, which ignores spaces and returns
`"visa"` if the first digit is 4, `"mastercard"` if it is 5, `"amex"` if it is 3, and `"unknown"` otherwise
(including for an empty string).
hints: Check `digits[:1]` (an empty slice is safe) against "4", "5" and "3".

tests.name: masks all but the last four
works without spaces and on short numbers
the brand from the first digit
strings come back
tests.code: assert isinstance(mask('12345678'), str) and isinstance(brand('4'), str)

tests.name: numbers of four digits or fewer are shown whole

steps.title: Check your understanding
steps.body: Work each one out before running anything.

questions.explanation: Positions 1, 2 and 3 are y, t, h; the slice stops before 4.
Strings are immutable; build a new one instead, e.g. `"b" + s[1:]`.
Counting from 0: b=0, a=1, n=2. `find` returns the first position.
`strip()` returns a new string; without `name = name.strip()` the original is unchanged.

steps.title: What you can do now
steps.body:
- Pick out characters by position, counting from 0 or from the end with negative numbers.
- Cut slices, knowing the end position is excluded and that out-of-range slices are safe.
- Use string methods, and keep their result, because strings never change in place.
- Loop over the characters or words of a text.

Next: lists, which look like strings but *can* change, and that changes everything.
